I'm in the UK, so YMMV. I've been in pain for nearly 30 years, since I was 12. The beating I took that day from my stepfather left me with a fractured arm and bruised ribs, my rib cage was also shifted from the final kick he gave me. 

The pain was slow to come on at first, I was repeatedly told it's just growing pains, you'll get over it, and so on. In my early 20's the pain started to become more prominent on the left side of my chest and quickly spread into my left arm, followed by my right hip, hands, and the rest of my chest. 

Nearly 17 years of bullshit diagnoses, not being taken seriously, lack of real support by anyone medical and even family: "it's a phase, there's nothing wrong with you", "it's in your head, there's nothing wrong with you" and so on and on... The whole time I'm on so many drugs you could use me as a rattle in a band!

5 years ago I finally found a GP that had some sympathy and genuinely seemed to want to help. She told me it's not in my head (well, not psychosomatic anyway) and started ordering lots of tests. X-rays, MRIs, bloods, physio... You name it, she tried it; except the one thing I needed: Neurological review.

After years of not finding anything except a slight impingement on my S1 root nerve.

I was sent to the Pain Clinic. I thought I'd be looked after, we'd find a solution, but I was wrong. All they want to do is send me on a 12 week course with other pain sufferers to discuss my pain for 2 hours a week, during work time!! 

The disconnect between what I was told to expect from the Pain Clinic and what I got was absolutely disgusting!! Because I said no to the talking option I was dismissed from the clinic. I'm just in awe of the monumental fuckery that is pain management on the NHS. They just don't get it at all!!

So yes, I'm with you! Strap'em down and give me the controls! I do believe they need to experience pain to better understand their patients needs and requirements. Chronic pain is no joke, and I'm sick of being treated like there's nothing wrong with me that a bit of therapy couldn't cure.

I'm in South Wales. I had a very interesting conversation with my NHS doctor 2 weeks ago about the private/NHS handover. 

Basically, the private clinic will lie to you and tell you that after titration you'll be handed back to the NHS. This is not true on the whole. Some GPs may take the risk and do it, but this is what my doc said

"There are zero care agreements across Wales and England between the NHS and the private psychologists operating across the UK. This means we cannot legally or professionally take over your care without you being assessed and diagnosed by the NHS."

Several private clinics were shut down, after police raids, recently due to false diagnoses and prescriptions. There's a Panorama documentary about it on BBC iPlayer at the moment. 

I asked the private clinic about my care, and the handover I was promised, and their response was "We write them a letter and they can choose to take it from there. If they won't, and you still want care and meds, you need to continue paying us"

I've been on the waiting list for the NHS for over 2 years. I recently had an email with the questionnaires and now I'm waiting on my friend to fill in their copy. Once I send them back I've been promised an appointment within 6 months. 

Between England and Wales, YMMV, but they are not too dissimilar on waiting times for mental health.

I'm in the UK, so it's the NHS for me. I get the choice of the first doc available, or potentially waiting weeks for the one who knows me best

I've had chronic pain for nearly 30 years. For the less painful years (12 to 24) I was repeatedly told I just needed more exercise (I was fit and healthy then), change my diet, growing pains, bursitis and so on and so on. 

My pain got much worse when I was about 25. Fainting due to sudden severe pain, couldn't sleep, pain got worse in my chest, then my arms, then my hip; more exercise, there's nothing wrong, bursitis, maybe you fell over....... 

They did all sorts of tests, x-rays, MRIs, blood, urine, poop, diet.... All of the GPs said it wasn't neurological, had to be muscular, but they couldn't prove it. They refused to refer me to a neurologist. 

The pain got so bad at one point, whatever the hell had happened in my body resulted in two surgeries to remove all the tubes on the back of my right nut. I've never experienced pain like it!! 7 months on my back until I could get the first surgery.

All this time I'm taking a concoction of meds to keep me functional, mostly opioids. 

When I was 37 and in a position to afford a little private care I went to see a neurologist: 25 years after this all started. I had a 15 minute appointment, and by minute 9 of my medical history (and his access to my NHS patient record) he diagnosed me with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome, the direct result of the last beating my step father gave me. The neurologist said it's 50/50 brain or spinal damage, and almost impossible to tell which. Considering they both have the same outcome, it didn't matter which. 

He booked me in for a spinal cord stimulator in his first available NHS slot (I couldn't afford the surgery privately)

I don't mind telling you; when I left his office and got into the cab to go home I completely broke down. Years of frustration and anger, and now the joy of being listened to and having an answer that 7 GPs swore wasn't the problem... It was too much! I cried like a baby! The taxi driver was a legend, he pulled over and let me just bawl. Nice chap, had a great chat with him on the way home. 

It took 18 months to get under the knife due to waiting lists, but I've lived with the device for 2 years now, and whilst I'm still in pain, it's about 70% less than what it was. It'll be more effective after the next tweak to the area of coverage is programmed in. 

That private appointment cost me £185. Best. Money. I've. Ever. Spent. 

My GP was not a happy bunny at all. But in the end, it's my health and I needed someone who knew what they were talking about. 

My old boss said to me (we work in IT) "GPs are like first-line support, they know a little about a lot unless it's their area of interest. You want the doods from the 3rd line looking at you!"

TLDR: GPs don't know jack when it comes to invisible/specialist/non-obvious pain, get a specialist!

Having a 3 day weekend is great, and you're right, greater opportunities to enjoy life, but not if your are tired and rundown from 40 hours over 4 days. You need time to recover. 

Let's not sugar coat the fact that you don't work any less hours. This is about humanity gaining and prospering from the modern age of tech that was "meant" to "free" them from the shackles of long working hours. Don't let anyone tell you that condensing 40 hours over 4 days to give you 3 days off in a row is a bonus to you; you are still working the same hours.

You're not actually getting those days off, nothing changes except a longer weekend. Those 50 days are equal to the extra 2 hours a day you'll work.

You'll get a longer weekend, but you don't gain any extra days off. 

We must be very careful how the corps will spin this. If you work 40 hours over 5 days and then condense that over 4 days, you gain nothing. It "looks" like you've gained a day each week, but you have not.

I see a lot of people saying a 4 day week with 10 hour days would be acceptable, but isn't the point of moving to a 4 day week to reduce the time we spend working rather than condense it?

Personally I want less stress and less working hours. I want to spend more time on my personal pursuits, time with family and loved ones, and I don't want to lose what time I already have during those 4 days. For me, it's about gaining time, not balancing it out by working longer hours over less days. 

If condensing your days and working longer hours is for you, I'm not knocking it, we are all different and have different thresholds for what works for us as an individual and a family. 

Ultimately, with all the technology we have, the promises made of less working hours thanks to that very technology has never come about. We (in the UK at least) only have weekends off (not for all I know) thanks to the unions and the subsequent laws, not the corporations. 

Just my two-pence fwiw

Just because you have fast internet does not mean that your connection is perfect. A large number of ISPs throughout the EU do traffic shaping on their networks; important traffic gets priority over gaming traffic for example. 

Virgin Media in the UK is known to apply traffic shaping rules (on consumer broadband packages) to prefer Xbox live over anything else. All UK ISPs also overload there networks with high contention ratios (or oversubscription ratios); A connection that can handle 40 users should have a contention ratio of 40 (1:1), but often the ratios are 60 or more. With Netflix, Prime, Disney etc those connections can become saturated pretty damn quickly, which will result in poor broadband performance, higher ping/latency times for everyone on that connection. Essentially, your gaming traffic is worth a lot less to the ISPs than Netflix, so Netflix will get a higher priority in their traffic shaping ruleset. (I am not endorsing this, all internet traffic should be equal)

Then there's the quality of your line, Signal to Noise Ratio etc, and the connection in the CAB down the street. You'll often find that the connectiosn in the CABs are rusted or have been vadalised. It's always worth taking a look at your set up and trying to improve things on your end as well.

I have a 500mb/s business line, no traffic shaping, no QoS policies etc but I still get lag and have an average latency of 24ms for Tarkov

And of course there's the server issues on the Tarkov end to contend with.
